title: Great Pyramid Alignment: How Did They Find True North?
hook: How did 4,500-year-old builders find true north without a compass?

scenes.narration: Stand at the foot of the Great Pyramid and look along its east or west side. That edge runs almost exactly north–south, off true north by only about three arcminutes, roughly a twentieth of a degree. <short pause> It was built in the 26th century BCE, finished around 2560 BCE. No compass. No satellites. So how did they do it?
scenes.caption: GIZA, c. 2560 BCE

scenes.label: average misalignment of the sides from true north
scenes.narration: That's about three arcminutes, if you like your units tiny. On a base more than two hundred and thirty metres long, it works out to a drift of only around twenty centimetres along a whole side. That's tighter than most of us could manage with a phone compass.
scenes.caption: 3 ARCMINUTES

scenes.narration: And a magnetic compass wouldn't have saved them. Today, an uncorrected compass at Giza points about five degrees east of true north. That's roughly a hundred times worse, and the figure shifts over time. Besides, compasses wouldn't turn up in this part of the world for thousands of years.
scenes.caption: NO COMPASS

scenes.heading: Two Suspects, One Witness
scenes.narration: So let's treat this like a case file. Two suspects: the stars and the sun's shadow. And one very surprising witness, a logbook written by a man named Merer. <short pause> We'll meet him last.
scenes.caption: THE CASE FILE

scenes.narration: First, the scene of the crime. The Giza plateau, on the Nile's west bank, just outside modern Cairo. Pharaoh Khufu's pyramid rose here, originally about 146 metres tall (about 139 today), from roughly two and a third million blocks. And before the first block went down, someone had to decide which way it would face.
scenes.caption: THE SCENE

scenes.narration: Suspect one: the night sky. Egyptian priests watched the stars closely. But there was no Polaris to point the way. The nearest naked-eye star, Thuban, was fairly faint and a couple of degrees off the pole, and true north was just empty sky.
scenes.caption: SUSPECT 1: STARS

events.label: Kate Spence proposes a star-pair method in Nature

scenes.narration: In 2000, Egyptologist Kate Spence suggested builders lined up two circumpolar stars, Kochab and Mizar, on a plumb line. That line pointed close to north, off by a small amount that depends on the date. <short pause> Her method implies later dates than most Egyptologists accept, which is one reason it's contested.
scenes.caption: THE STAR TRICK

scenes.narration: Here's why her idea got attention. Spence argued that the small errors in Egypt's pyramids shift in step with their dates. And stars do slowly drift, which would leave exactly that kind of fingerprint. It's a clever idea, though not every Egyptologist is convinced.
scenes.caption: THE FINGERPRINT

scenes.label: for Earth's axis to complete one slow wobble (about 26,000)
scenes.narration: Here's the physics: Earth wobbles like a spinning top, once every roughly 26,000 years. Over the decades of pyramid-building, the sky creeps enough to shift where the stars sit relative to north.
scenes.caption: THE WOBBLE

scenes.narration: Suspect two: the shadow. All you need is a straight stick on flat ground. Mark where its shadow tip falls in the morning, and draw a circle around the stick through that mark. In the afternoon, the shadow tip touches the circle again. Mark that too.
scenes.delivery: clear and step-by-step, a little playful
scenes.caption: SUSPECT 2: SHADOW

scenes.narration: Draw a line between those two marks and it runs east to west. Cut it at a right angle, and there's north. Cheap, simple, and accurate to a fraction of a degree if you're careful. Engineer Glen Dash tested a version of it at Giza, and has argued it fits the pyramid's error well, though this too is debated.
scenes.caption: THE SHADOW LINE

scenes.heading: The Witness
scenes.subheading: A diary from the building site
scenes.narration: So, stars or shadows? The pyramid itself won't say. But in 2013, archaeologists found a witness who could tell us how that building site really worked.
scenes.caption: PLOT TWIST

scenes.narration: On the Red Sea coast, at an ancient harbour called Wadi al-Jarf, a team led by Pierre Tallet and Gregory Marouard found hundreds of papyrus fragments piled at the entrance to a closed storage gallery. They're the oldest inscribed papyri yet found. Among them was the logbook of an official named Merer.
scenes.caption: WADI AL-JARF, 2013

scenes.label: in Merer's boat crew, roughly
scenes.narration: Merer was an inspector in charge of a crew of about forty men. His diary reads like a work log: dull, practical, and priceless. Boats loaded, boats moved, days counted.
scenes.caption: INSPECTOR MERER

scenes.narration: And here's what he logged. Crews cut fine white limestone at Tura, on the Nile's east bank. Merer's boats carried it downriver to Giza, to a site the texts call the Horizon of Khufu. That stone was the smooth outer casing, and the diary shows trips repeating again and again.
scenes.caption: TURA TO GIZA

scenes.unit: km to Giza (approx.; Aswan by river)
scenes.narration: Why Tura? Giza's own rock made the rough inner core. Tura, about fifteen kilometres as the crow flies, gave better stone for the finish. And the granite for the inner chambers? That came from Aswan, roughly seven hundred kilometres in a straight line, and over eight hundred by river.
scenes.caption: WHERE STONE CAME FROM

scenes.narration: The Nile was the highway. Researchers think that during the yearly flood, the water crept close to the plateau, so boats could unload almost at the building site. Without that river, building it would have been far harder.
scenes.caption: THE NILE HIGHWAY

events.label: The pyramid's casing is nearly finished

scenes.narration: Merer's entries date to late in Khufu's reign, when the pyramid was close to complete. So no, the diary never mentions north. <short pause> But it shows a state running like clockwork, with inspectors, schedules and supply lines. A system that organised can surely run a survey.
scenes.caption: WHAT THE DIARY SAYS

scenes.narration: So, the verdict? Nobody has a signed confession. Scholars are still divided. Some favour stars, some favour the sun's shadow, and some think builders may have used both to cross-check.
scenes.caption: THE VERDICT

scenes.label: as the tallest human-made structure on Earth (as usually stated)
scenes.narration: And it worked. For roughly thirty-eight hundred years, it is usually said, the Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure, until Lincoln Cathedral's spire, around 1311, overtook it.
scenes.caption: STILL STANDING

scenes.narration: Remember the twentieth of a degree? It took careful observation, sticks, string and a river full of boats, all coordinated by people with no compass at all. The Great Pyramid isn't just big. It's remarkably precise, and it was built on a Nile supply chain.
scenes.caption: ALIGNED TO NORTH

scenes.heading: Which Suspect Do You Pick?
scenes.narration: Stars, shadows, or a bit of both? Tell me your pick in the comments. And if you like the stories behind the map, stick around for the next one.
scenes.caption: YOUR VERDICT

description:
How did the builders of the Great Pyramid of Giza find true north in the 26th century BCE, without a compass? We map Giza, test the star and shadow theories, and follow the Merer diary papyrus, which records limestone shipped from Tura along the Nile.

Explore the leading ideas behind the Great Pyramid's near-perfect alignment: the Kochab and Mizar star method, the shadow-and-stick method, and what the oldest inscribed papyri tell us about how the building site really ran.

Sources to check:
- Pierre Tallet and Mark Lehner, "The Red Sea Scrolls" (Thames & Hudson, 2021)
- Kate Spence, "Ancient Egyptian chronology and the astronomical orientation of pyramids," Nature, 2000
- Glen Dash's papers on the Giza plateau survey, Journal of Ancient Egyptian Architecture
- Flinders Petrie, "The Pyramids and Temples of Gizeh" (1883)

Animation and narration are AI-assisted; script reviewed by a human.
